lead: An internal combustion engine burns its fuel inside its own cylinder. The hot gas pushes a piston or a rotor, and a shaft carries the work out. Burning inside avoids the pipe and chimney losses of a steam plant, so the engine is small, light and starts in seconds; that is why it sits in scooters, gensets and pump sets. No two engines are alike, so engineers sort them by a few independent choices: ignition, number of strokes, cooling, aspiration and fuel. This chapter gives the short history of those choices and the labels that follow from them.
prereq: You need nothing earlier in this book; school-level physics on pressure, volume and the crank is enough.

sections.h3: Four names that made the engine

blocks.text: In a steam engine, coal burns in a separate furnace and the heat travels through boiler tubes into steam. Much of it escapes up the chimney, and the boiler is heavy. An internal combustion engine (IC engine) puts the flame next to the moving part. Almost all the heat is released in the gas that does the pushing, so the engine is light enough for a two-wheeler.
Four people are asked for by name:

items: Étienne Lenoir, 1860: the first IC engine built in large numbers. It ran on coal gas, was lit by a flame, and did not compress the charge before burning, so its efficiency was very low.

Nikolaus Otto, 1876: compressed the charge first, then lit it, in four piston strokes. Compression is the step that makes an IC engine efficient, and almost every petrol engine still follows his sequence; see four-stroke operation.
Rudolf Diesel, patent 1892, working engine 1897: squeezed air so hard that it became hot enough to set fire to fuel sprayed into it, so no spark was needed.
Dugald Clerk, 1878: a two-stroke engine with a separate pump to fill and sweep the cylinder, giving one power stroke every revolution.

blocks.text: A reciprocating engine has a piston sliding in a cylinder, a connecting rod, and a crank that turns the back-and-forth motion into rotation. Nearly every road vehicle uses this shape.

A rotary engine has no piston that stops and reverses. The Wankel engine has a triangular rotor turning inside a curved housing. Each face of the rotor traps a pocket of gas and carries it through suction, compression, expansion and exhaust in one continuous turn. It is smooth and compact, but sealing the rotor tips against the housing is difficult, so few cars use it now.

The two families are classified apart because the moving part, and the way the chamber volume changes, are different. Ignition, fuel and cooling labels apply inside both families. Part names are in Chapter 1.2.

Classification is several lists, not one. An engine takes one label from each list, and the choices are independent: a two-stroke engine can be air-cooled or water-cooled, spark-ignited or compression-ignited. Changing one label does not force a change in another.

items: Ignition. In a spark-ignition (SI) engine a spark plug lights a mixture of fuel and air prepared earlier. In a compression-ignition (CI) engine, fuel is sprayed into air that compression has made hot, and it ignites by itself. See SI and CI working principle.
Strokes. A four-stroke engine uses four piston strokes and two shaft revolutions per cycle. A two-stroke engine uses ports and scavenging, and fires once per revolution. See Chapter 1.3.
Cooling. An air-cooled engine has fins on the cylinder and loses heat to air blown past them. A water-cooled engine has a coolant jacket around the cylinder and a radiator.

Aspiration. A naturally aspirated engine fills its cylinder at about atmospheric pressure. A supercharged or turbocharged engine uses a compressor to push in denser air, so more fuel burns in the same swept volume. See Unit 4, Cooling, Lubrication and Supercharging.
Fuel. Petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG, alcohol blends and hydrogen are all used in production engines.

blocks.text: Two more descriptions are often added: the number and layout of cylinders (single, inline, V, opposed) and the duty (steady genset, variable-speed vehicle). Neither is a stroke label. Two-stroke counts strokes per cycle; two-cylinder counts cylinders.
Petrol with spark ignition: scooters, motorcycles, cars and small gensets. Petrol mixes with air easily and the spark fixes the moment of burning.

Diesel with compression ignition: trucks, buses, tractors and irrigation pump sets, where the engine runs for long hours and fuel cost per kilometre matters. CNG runs city buses and autorickshaws where a gas pipeline and filling stations exist; its high octane rating lets an SI engine use a higher compression ratio.

Two-stroke: small scooters, chainsaws, outboard motors and some gensets. Fewer parts and one power stroke per turn make it cheap and lively, but fresh charge escapes with the exhaust, so it is smoky; stricter emission rules moved most Indian two-wheelers to four-stroke.

Air cooling suits motorcycles, scooters and small portable gensets, where there is no radiator to service. Water cooling suits cars, trucks, tractors and any large engine that must hold a steady temperature under load.

figure.caption: The tree sorts engines by ignition, by stroke and by cooling; the note on the root adds the fourth axis, aspiration. Each branch is a separate question, so any leaf can be paired with any leaf on another branch.

spec.aria: A classification tree sorts IC engines by ignition into SI and CI, by stroke into four-stroke and two-stroke, and by cooling into air and water, with aspiration noted as a fourth axis.

examples.question: A scooter engine carries these particulars: fuel petrol, spark plug, two-stroke, cooling by fins, no blower or turbocharger, displacement 150 cm³, one cylinder. (a) Classify it under five headings. (b) Name one vehicle use. (c) How many power strokes does this cylinder make in 1000 revolutions of the crankshaft, and how many would a four-stroke cylinder of the same size make?
steps: Ignition: a spark plug lights a prepared mixture, so the engine is spark-ignition (SI).
Strokes: the engine is stated to be two-stroke, so it gives one power stroke per crankshaft revolution.
Cooling: fins and no radiator or coolant pump, so it is air-cooled.
Aspiration: no blower or turbocharger is fitted, so it is naturally aspirated.
Use: a scooter, and equally a small motorcycle or a portable pump.
Two-stroke power strokes: 1000 revolutions × 1 power stroke per revolution = 1000 power strokes.
Four-stroke power strokes: one stroke per 2 revolutions, so 1000 ÷ 2 = 500 power strokes.
The displacement of 150 cm³ and the single cylinder fix the size only; they change none of the five labels.
examples.answer: Petrol, SI, two-stroke, air-cooled, naturally aspirated; used in a scooter; 1000 power strokes in 1000 revolutions against 500 for a four-stroke of the same size.
examples.check:
rev = 1000
two_stroke = rev * 1
four_stroke = rev // 2
print(two_stroke)
print(four_stroke)

traps: Two-stroke is not two-cylinder. A single-cylinder two-stroke engine exists; the label counts piston strokes per cycle, not cylinders.
Diesel is a fuel and a cycle name, while compression ignition is a method. Most diesel engines are CI, but an ignition question wants the words SI or CI.
Air-cooled does not mean uncooled. The fins, a fan, or the rush of air past a moving motorcycle carry the heat away.
Supercharged and turbocharged both mean forced aspiration. In a turbocharger the compressor is driven by an exhaust turbine; in a supercharger it is driven by a belt or gears from the crankshaft.
A four-stroke cylinder fires once in two revolutions, not once per revolution. Halve the revolution count before you count power strokes.

quiz.q: Who built the first internal combustion engine produced in large numbers, and what fuel did it use?
quiz.a: Étienne Lenoir, about 1860. It burned coal gas, was lit by a flame, and did not compress the charge.

quiz.q: Define SI and CI engines in one line each.
quiz.a: SI: a spark plug ignites a prepared fuel-air mixture. CI: fuel is sprayed into air heated by compression and ignites by itself.

quiz.q: Why did compressing the charge before ignition make Otto's engine better than Lenoir's?
quiz.a: Compression raises the pressure and temperature at the start of burning. The same fuel then delivers more work during expansion and less heat is lost, so efficiency rises.

quiz.q: A genset engine is diesel-fuelled, four-stroke, water-cooled and turbocharged. Classify it under four headings and find the power strokes per cylinder in 2000 revolutions.
quiz.a: Ignition CI (diesel fuel), four-stroke, water-cooled, forced aspiration (turbocharged). A four-stroke fires once in two revolutions: 2000 ÷ 2 = 1000 power strokes.

quiz.q: A two-wheeler is sold as "150 cm³, four-stroke, air-cooled". Which classification labels are still missing, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: Ignition and aspiration are missing, and the fuel is not stated. Petrol and SI are likely but must be confirmed; natural or forced aspiration changes the power available from the same 150 cm³.

quiz.q: Engine A: petrol, SI, two-stroke, air-cooled, 100 cm³. Engine B: diesel, CI, four-stroke, water-cooled, turbocharged, 3000 cm³. Match each to a scooter and a highway truck, with reasons.
quiz.a: A is the scooter: light, cheap, air cooling suits a moving vehicle, and the two-stroke gives high power per cm³. B is the truck: CI gives torque and fuel economy over long hauls, water cooling holds temperature under sustained load, and the turbocharger pushes in enough air mass to pull a loaded truck.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to call a Wankel engine a four-stroke engine?
quiz.a: There is no piston and no stroke. A rotor face carries a chamber through four phases continuously, so the cycle has four phases but is not made of four strokes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research engines now use more than four strokes: five-stroke designs use extra cylinders to recover exhaust energy, and split-cycle engines separate compression from expansion into different cylinders. Free-piston linear generators and better-sealed rotary engines return in hybrid form. Search terms: split-cycle engine, five-stroke engine, free-piston engine, Wankel sealing.
